title: Write-Through, Write-Back and the Dirty Bit
unit: Memory Interfacing, Hierarchy and Cache Mapping
quickIdea: On a write hit, write-through updates memory as well and write-back marks the line dirty; on a write miss, write-allocate loads the block first and no-write-allocate writes straight to memory.
remember: Write-through: every write goes to the cache and to memory, so memory is always current and no block is ever dirty. Cost: memory traffic on every write.
Write-back: the write updates only the cache and sets the dirty (modified) bit; memory is updated when the dirty line is evicted. Cost: a dirty bit per line and a write-back on eviction.
Write-allocate: on a write miss, fetch the block into the cache and then write it. No-write-allocate: write to memory and leave the cache alone.
The common pairing is write-back with write-allocate and write-through with no-write-allocate, but all four combinations are legal.
A write-back cache can evict a dirty block on a read miss as well as a write miss, and that eviction costs an extra memory write that the miss penalty must include.

example.prompt: GATE CSE 2024 Set 1 Q.43: WBC is write-back and WTC is write-through, both set-associative with LRU. Which statements are true - (A) a read miss in WBC never evicts a dirty block, (B) a read miss in WTC never triggers a write-back, (C) a write hit in WBC can modify the dirty bit, (D) a write miss in WTC always writes the victim block to memory before loading?
example.work: A: LRU picks a victim by recency with no exemption for dirty lines, so a read miss can evict a dirty block - false. B: no WTC block is ever dirty, so eviction never needs a write-back - true. C: a write hit sets the dirty bit to 1 - true. D: the victim in WTC is already clean, so it need not be written - false.

gateAngle: GATE asks this as a statement-selection question, and every statement turns on one of two facts: write-through leaves nothing dirty, and LRU does not protect dirty lines. Learn those two and the four statements decide themselves.

variations.label: VERIFIED PYQ
variations.question: GATE CSE 2024 Set 1 Q.43, as worked above.
variations.why: The false statements both assume a protection that does not exist: LRU does not spare dirty lines, and a clean victim never needs writing back.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: A write-back cache with write-allocate takes a write miss on a full set. List the memory operations the miss may cause.
variations.answer: A read to fetch the missed block, plus a write of the victim if it is dirty, plus the write of the new data later when that line is itself evicted.
variations.why: It makes the miss penalty of a write-back cache a sum rather than a single fetch, which is the arithmetic version of the same concept.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: Why is write-through usually paired with no-write-allocate?
variations.answer: Because a write-through cache gains nothing from holding a block it has just written - memory already has the data - so fetching the block on a write miss is pure cost.
variations.why: It explains the pairing as a consequence rather than a convention to memorise.

trap.what: Believing a write-through cache needs a dirty bit.
trap.why: Memory is updated on every write, so no line ever differs from memory; there is nothing for a dirty bit to record.
trap.counterexample: A write-through cache that sets a dirty bit would write back a block that memory already holds, doubling the traffic for no correctness gain.

check.question: A write-back cache with 94% of its lines dirty is flushed. What must happen, and how does it compare with a write-through cache?
check.answer: Every dirty line must be written to memory before eviction; a write-through cache needs no flush at all because memory is already current.
check.explanation: The flush cost is the price write-back pays for its lower steady-state traffic - which is why write-back is preferred for long-running programs and write-through for simple or shared-memory designs.
